name: Mengdi Xu

papers.title: Dex-X: Learning Visual-Tactile Dexterous Manipulation From Human Demonstration with Simulated Interaction
papers.abstract: Human videos are an abundant source of dexterous manipulation behaviors, but they lack tactile information that is crucial for contact-rich interaction. This raises a fundamental question: can robots learn deployable visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies directly from human video demonstrations? We present Dex-X, a framework for learning visual-tactile dexterous manipulation from human videos through simulation. Our key insight is that simulation can serve as a tactile completion engine. Given monocular human demonstrations, Dex-X reconstructs hand-object interactions in simulation, where physically grounded contact dynamics provide tactile supervision unavailable in the original videos. Leveraging this recovered tactile information, we train visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies and distill them into deployable policies operating on point-cloud observations and tactile sensing. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on dexterous hand-arm platforms across diverse grasping and contact-rich tool-use tasks.  The teacher policy achieves 65.9% average success across eight tasks in simulation, while the distilled visual-tactile policy achieves a 53% success rate on cube picking and 23% on the challenging real-world table-cleaning task, which is not achieved by existing general sim-to-real manipulation systems. Our results suggest that tactile completion is a critical ingredient for scalable dexterous manipulation learning and provide a path toward learning real-world robot skills from Internet-scale human video data.

papers.title: Humanoid Badminton: Learning Dynamic Racket Skills from Limited Human Motion Data
papers.abstract:
High-speed racket sports provide a demanding testbed for humanoid robots, where successful interaction requires time-critical decisions, precise striking, and dynamic whole-body coordination. This challenge becomes especially pronounced in badminton, as the shuttlecock follows highly nonlinear trajectories and each return requires tightly coordinated contact selection, racket control, and balance recovery within a short time window. Although human demonstrations offer valuable motion priors for such athletic skills, available badminton data is often limited and imperfect; meanwhile, purely task-driven reinforcement learning can optimize returns but tends to produce unnatural motions that are difficult to deploy on hardware.
To address these challenges, we present a three-stage hierarchical framework for athletic humanoid badminton that combines human motion priors with task-driven optimization. The framework first learns a compact latent skill space from retargeted human demonstrations, then optimizes skill composition through reinforcement learning, and finally regularizes the learned behavior with a context-conditioned adversarial latent prior to promote human-like motion. When deployed on a real humanoid robot, our system demonstrates multi-skill badminton play with human players, including rallies and jump smashes. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first real-world demonstration of humanoid jump-smash skills in racket sports.

papers.title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data
papers.abstract: Exploiting symmetry in robot policy learning requires knowing how a symmetry group operates on observations and actions, an assumption that often breaks in partially observable MDPs (POMDPs) with pixel observations, where this operation is nonlinear and difficult to specify by hand. Existing approaches sidestep this challenge using environment-specific preprocessing, limiting portability across tasks and observation modalities. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that discovers how a symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in POMDPs directly from offline interaction data, while explicitly enforcing the group axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop tasks, MIRROR attains the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61% reduction in compatibility error over LaLiGAN, the strongest GAN baseline on that metric. The discovered operations instantiate an equivariant behavior cloning (BC) policy that outperforms vanilla BC on all four tasks, with per-task gains up to 9.66%, and the same framework transfers zero-shot to a real Kinova GEN3 arm under a different observation modality. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io/review/.
